To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

white avoidance of predominantly non-white areas and white out-movement, as well as white in-movement to white areas, contribute to the maintenance of high levels of white/ black segregation in New York.
the odds of white in-movement are significantly lower in mixed and non-white areas, while the odds of Hispanic and black in-movement are substantially higher.

the persistence of extreme levels of white-black segregation in New York is due in large part to white avoidance of black areas, and the production of predominantly non-white areas that are predominantly Hispanic and predominantly black, are the result of the same avoidance behavior.
In summary, our research is concerned with

understanding the micro-level processes that help explain the persistence of extreme levels of white-black segregation in New York, and the emergence of areas composed almost exclusively by blacks and Hispanics.
the micro-level mobility processes that maintain the high levels of white-black segregation in New York.
how the racial/ethnic composition of an area affects the odds of mobility, and how the odds of mobility in turn affect the racial/ethnic makeup of a neighborhood.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
white flight and avoidance are the primary mechanisms for maintaining extreme levels of white and black segregation.
the micro-level dynamics that maintain extreme levels of segregation in New York are a function of both white avoidance of non-white areas and white out-movement.
white avoidance and flight are important mechanisms in the persistence of white/black segregation and the production of predominantly non-white areas dominated by black and Hispanic residents.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
housing mobility is the key to understanding racial/ethnic residential segregation in the United States, but that the dynamics are not as simple as the traditional “white flight” hypothesis suggests.

the micro-level dynamics that maintain extreme levels of black/white segregation are not the same as the micro-level dynamics responsible for extreme levels of Hispanic/white segregation, and that the micro-level processes that produce predominantly black areas and predominantly Hispanic areas are different as well.

white avoidance of predominantly black and mixed areas, coupled with black avoidance of predominantly Hispanic areas, is the key to understanding the persistence of high levels of white-black segregation.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the dynamics that maintain segregation are not only about white avoidance of black neighborhoods, but also about the persistence of black/white and white/Hispanic segregation.
white avoidance of black neighborhoods, coupled with white flight from these same areas, are key processes in maintaining the high levels of white-black segregation in New York.

the micro-level mobility processes that have produced and sustained the city’s racial/ethnic residential segregation are not simply the result of whites avoiding non-white areas, but rather the result of whites and non-whites avoiding one another.
